War in Ukraine: Deadly Russian air raid on Kramatorsk leaves 1 dead and 17 wounded Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 14/08/2026 - 16:22 GMT+2 At least one person was killed and 17 injured in a Russian airstrike on Kramatorsk in eastern Ukraine overnight, according to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service. … More Emergency crews worked through the night on Friday to rescue residents trapped under rubble and extinguish fires after eight FAB‑250 guided aerial bombs hit the city, local authorities said. Several private homes and a garage caught fire, while an apartment building suffered extensive damage. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT The strike caused sections of the ten‑storey apartment building from the first to the sixth floors to collapse, the emergency service said. Rescuers were filmed pulling a woman and a man from the rubble and helping residents leave damaged buildings. Firefighters also tackled flames at several sites across the city, while cars were damaged near the impact areas. The Donetsk regional prosecutor’s office has opened a war‑crimes investigation into the attack. Kramatorsk has repeatedly come under Russian attacks during the war because of its proximity to the front line. The injured, aged between 47 and 85, were treated for blast and traumatic brain injuries, shrapnel wounds, cuts and abrasions, officials said. https://www.rferl.org/a/poland-financial.text: Accessibility links Skip to main content Skip to main Navigation Skip to Search Print Options: Images Multimedia Embedded Content Comments News Poland Offers Financial Incentives To US As Talks On Military Base Advance, Minister Tells RFE/RL By Alex Raufoglu September 26, 2026 00:29 CET Poland Offers Financial Incentives To US As Talks On Military Base Advance, Minister Tells RFE/RL Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk (left) and US President Donald Trump. (file photo) WASHINGTON -- Poland is offering to pay $15,000 a year for every US soldier stationed on its territory and cover infrastructure costs as Warsaw and Washington move closer to agreeing on establishing a permanent American military base, a senior Polish defense official told RFE/RL. Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski said in an interview in Washington on September 25 that negotiations with the Pentagon are now focused on how to implement the plan, including the forces, capabilities, and possible locations involved. “We are discussing with the Pentagon different variations of the execution of the decision,” Zalewski said. While declining to say which US units could be deployed or where, Zalewski disclosed new details of Poland’s offer to Washington. “We are offering very special conditions for American troops,” he said. Embed share Tusk Says Poland On High Alert After Russian Strikes Near Ukraine's Western Border by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:47 0:00 “We will cover the costs of infrastructure. We are also covering the cost of each American soldier stationing in Poland by $15,000 per year.” Asked who would pay, Zalewski replied: “It’s paid by the Polish taxpayers.” The offer underscores Warsaw’s determination to secure a permanent US military presence as the Pentagon reviews the deployment of American forces across Europe. President Donald Trump said on September 17 that progress was being made toward establishing a US Army base in Poland and that its location could be announced soon. The United States already has thousands of troops in Poland, mostly on a rotational basis, and the country has become a major hub for NATO operations along the alliance’s eastern flank. SEE ALSO: On NATO's Doorstep: The Checkpoints Being Targeted Along Ukraine's Borders Zalewski said the details of any permanent deployment remain under negotiation and are being discussed in the context of Washington’s broader review of its European military posture. “We are discussing different variants, different variations of troops, of capabilities, of locations,” he said, adding that Warsaw expects greater clarity after the review is completed. The Pentagon did not immediately respond to requests for comment. For Warsaw, the significance of a permanent base goes beyond the number of troops stationed there. “Permanent bases create permanent commitment,” Zalewski said, adding such a deployment would be less dependent on changes in the political or military environment while also sending a direct signal to Moscow. An attack on Poland, he said, would risk bringing Russian forces into direct conflict with US troops. “It makes a very important, urgent message to [Russian] President [Vladimir] Putin that the US has strategic interests in Poland, and that attack on Poland would be the attack on US armed forces in Poland,” Zalewski said. Polish Defense Official: Russia 'Escalating Acts Of Terror In Poland' by RFE/RL No media source currently available 0:00 0:00:37 0:00 He also argued that a permanent US presence should not be seen simply as Washington doing Warsaw a favor. “This permanent base is not the outcome of a certain kind of altruism,” he said, but reflects “very well understood American interests.” Poland has rapidly expanded its military and invested heavily in American weapons systems. The two countries have also deepened energy ties, including cooperation with US companies on Poland’s first nuclear power plant. SEE ALSO: Amid Russian Provocations And Warnings Over Possible Attack, Europe Mulls Contingency Plans Security experts said a permanent base would strengthen Washington’s commitment to NATO’s eastern flank but cautioned that its significance would depend partly on what happens to US forces elsewhere in Europe. “A permanent US base in Poland would be an important signal of American commitment to NATO’s eastern flank, especially as Washington reviews its wider military posture in Europe,” David Cattler, a former NATO assistant secretary-general for intelligence and security, told RFE/RL. But Cattler, now a senior fellow at the Center for European Policy Analysis, said allies would be watching the broader outcome of the US review. “Allies will judge the whole picture: what forces and capabilities remain, how quickly they can reinforce Poland and the Baltic states, and whether they can operate together effectively,” he said. “A base would strengthen deterrence if it adds real capability to the eastern flank. It would do far less to reassure allies if accompanied by substantial US reductions elsewhere in Europe.” Matthew Boyse, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute and former US deputy assistant secretary of state for European and Eurasian affairs, said the negotiations reflected Poland’s growing role in NATO. SEE ALSO: Baltic States Arm For Russian Threat As Leaked Letter Shows Growing Fears “These base talks showcase Poland’s continuing value as a major NATO ally,” Boyse told RFE/RL. Poland has sharply increased defense spending in recent years and has emerged as one of NATO’s biggest military spenders relative to the size of its economy. “Instead of complaining about ‘reliability,’ Poland is pulling out the stops,” Boyse said. “The administration sees and appreciates that.” Charles Kupchan, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the prospect of a permanent base would be welcomed in countries closest to Russia but cautioned that uncertainty remains over Washington’s broader approach to Europe. “The prospect of a permanent US base in Poland is good news for Poles and others along NATO’s eastern flank, especially amid growing concern about the threat posed by Russia,” Kupchan told RFE/RL. “Nonetheless, this is still a time of uncertainty for NATO,” he said, citing Trump’s sometimes contentious relationship with allies and the Pentagon review that could reduce the US presence elsewhere in Europe. Warsaw’s push for a permanent American presence comes as Russia appears increasingly willing to take risks against NATO members. “Russia’s readiness to accept higher risk is visible, and Russia is ready to escalate,” Zalewski said. He pointed to recent incidents that Poland has linked to Russia, including airspace violations and alleged acts of sabotage, saying they illustrated the pressure facing countries on NATO’s eastern flank. Poland, he said, is responding both through its alliance with the United States and through NATO. For Warsaw, a permanent American base would add another layer to that deterrence by making clear that any military confrontation involving Poland could immediately involve US forces. “Permanent bases create permanent commitment,” Zalewski said. https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-12/t.text: Explore the ABC analysis Trump shifts position on Ukraine as fuel prices pose existential threat L By Laura Tingle Topic: World Politics Posted Mon 12 Oct 2026 at 3:23pm Mon 12 Oct 2026 at 3:23pm Mon 12 Oct 2026 at 3:23pm Recent comments by Donald Trump have put distance between him and Ukraine. ( Reuters: Eric Lee ) abc.net.au/news/trump-russia-ukraine-energy/107255500 Link copied Share Share article It would be easy to dismiss the erratic, contradictory and increasingly rapid changes in the proclamations from Donald Trump about Ukraine, and US diesel purchases from Russia, if it wasn't for the US making threats to Europe about cutting intelligence and military procurements to Ukraine. The underlying shift amid all the noise appears to be one of Trump moving back from his position of recent months to align more with Russia than Ukraine in their long running war. But it is hard to see this as a clear strategic change by the US and not one driven principally by the almost existential threat posed to the Republican Party in the looming US mid-term elections by soaring fuel prices. "This is hard to accept, I know. But Trump just makes things up," John Bolton, Trump's former national security adviser, told The Telegraph in the UK. "This is not about Ukraine and Russia. This is about the American election. The whole point of the diesel deal, which is stunning and outrageous itself, but the whole point of that is to get diesel flowing internationally, specifically into the US market to get prices down." Analyst Nigel Gould-Davies, a senior fellow for Russia and Eurasia at International Institute for Strategic Studies, said the US "resembles a giant flailing in quicksand. Its policy is sinking under the weight of its own contradictions". International strategy driven by domestic politics is only made murkier by revelations in recent weeks of the deal in the offing involving a conglomerate linked to the Trump family seeking to buy the oil assets of a major Russian oligarch. It's been just a month since Trump told Ukraine it "has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia", arguing it was the Russia-Ukraine war, rather than the Middle East, that had pushed US diesel prices above $US6 a gallon for the first time. Ukrainian strikes have been systematically targeting Russia's oil refineries. ( Reuters ) Then, in an unfortunate bit of timing for Trump, the US House of Representatives passed new sanction laws on Russia and Iran which required tariffs of up to 100 per cent on the biggest buyers of Russian crude and gas. A week later, Trump was pressuring Europe to release its diesel reserves , threatening a ban on US diesel exports. With the G7 agreeing to release up to 100 million barrels from strategic reserves over four months, the US president asserted that a US export ban was "never really on the table". This month, there has been an executive order to let tax-free, red-dyed off-road diesel be used on public roads. Even Trump told a rally he wasn't sure what that meant. Then on Friday, after a phone call with Vladamir Putin, Trump announced Russia would supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, 500,000 tons in November, then 1 million tons, then another 3 million tons, but said nothing about how this would happen given the sanctions regime, or the war. The US Treasury immediately issued a licence suspending US sanctions on Russian diesel until April next year. Critics said the US-Russia diesel deal would help Moscow pay for its offensive in Ukraine. ( Reuters: Sputnik/Gavriil Grigorov/Pool ) Most analysts say the amounts of diesel involved are not substantial enough to change prices, and the International Energy Agency estimates Russian diesel output has fallen by about 30 per cent anyway. The White House also hasn't said who would be paying for the diesel. Ukraine took an understandably dim view of the deal, saying it was a gift to Putin that would only prolong the war by helping finance Russia's military campaign. Just to broaden out the ramifications of keeping the Russian war machine alive, it came amid reports by Bloomberg that Russia had provided Iran with missiles, allowing Tehran to replenish its arsenals amid uncertainty over the possibility of renewed US strikes on Iran. So Russia is reportedly arming the state with which Trump is at war: a war that kicked off the fuel crisis in the first place. Loading There were more presidential outbursts over the weekend after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticised the deal. Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president". "I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does", he said, adding Zelenskyy "wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel". Several European leaders emerged to express their support for Zelenskyy, saying they would seek to increase economic pressure on Russia after the deal was announced. Leaders from the EU, the UK, France, Germany and Poland all reiterated their support. UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said "we are trying to increase economic pressure on Russia, not to give President Putin any sense of a weakening of Western resolve, which remains absolute". More on Ukraine Ukraine says Starlink at normal speed after delays impede military Topic: Unrest, Conflict and War Ukraine says Starlink at normal speed after delays impede military Topic: Unrest, Conflict and War Melania Trump says she brokered ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky Topic: Unrest, Conflict and War Zelenskyy says fresh Russian strikes show 'no change' in Kremlin position Topic: World Politics Putin agrees to resume peace talks with Ukraine and US Topic: World Politics Back in the US, the diesel deal angered members of his own party, who joined with Democrats in claiming that it was against the law. Seven senators, including four Republicans, on Sunday called on the US president to "immediately reverse course" on his deal to purchase millions of tons of diesel fuel from Moscow, calling it a "financial lifeline" to a murderous regime. Then overnight, Trump announced on Truth Social that, "effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine". He gave no details. The ceasefire seemed to be news to both Russia and Ukraine . Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure continued after the announcement. Zelenskyy responds to Trump's election call The US president has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for high diesel prices. But what is of more concern than the war of words is the fact the US has been threatening to not only stop intelligence sharing with Ukraine but to stop the deal which allows Ukraine to buy weapons from the US through NATO. The Financial Times reported that the US told European countries over the weekend it might stop selling the weapons if Ukraine continued to strike Russian refineries. "They are calling Kyiv … they are calling everyone [in Europe]," the FT reported an official who received a call from a US defence official as saying. The announcement of the diesel deal came as Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were meeting with Ukrainian negotiators, who heard about the deal as they sat down. The FT also reported that these threats were made to the negotiators. "It was a firm request from POTUS", one of the Ukrainians involved in the talks told the FT, referring to Trump. On the one hand, world leaders seem inured to, and often just irritated by, Trump's increasing rages at the windmill as he confronts a potential political meltdown on November 3. But the threats on intelligence sharing and weapons purchases provide a new test of how the rest of the west, let alone Ukraine, responds. Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.
